summary.text: A coastal flood is an event in which seawater submerges dry, low-lying land along a coast.
It can be set off by storm surges from hurricanes and tropical cyclones, by sea-level rise from climate change, or by tsunamis.
Beyond deaths, these floods cause injuries, spread infectious diseases through dirty water, and can leave anxiety, depression and PTSD that can last months or years.

facts.label: Three flood paths
facts.value: Direct flooding, overtopping, or breaching a barrier

facts.label: Tsunami triggers
facts.value: Earthquakes, landslides, volcanic eruptions, glacier calving

facts.label: Diseases it spreads
facts.value: Cholera, dengue, malaria, typhoid and others

facts.label: Most vulnerable to trauma
facts.value: Children, older adults, socially isolated people

items.prompt: Weeks after a coastal flood, a town sees a jump in cholera and diarrhoeal illness. What most likely drives this?

options.label: Cold seawater weakening people's immunity
Salt spray carried inland by the wind
Contaminated water and poor sanitation
Loud storms disturbing people's sleep

items.explain: Floods contaminate water and break down sanitation, which spreads diseases such as cholera and diarrhoeal illness.

items.prompt: A man with heart disease comes through a coastal flood unhurt, yet his condition worsens in the weeks after. Why?

options.label: His medicines and medical care were disrupted
Breathing sea air strains the heart
Floodwater salt enters the bloodstream
The low tide after floods lowers blood pressure

items.explain: Floods can worsen chronic illnesses like heart disease by cutting off access to medications and healthcare.

items.prompt: A tsunami rolls into a town. Besides its height and speed, what makes it so destructive as it flows over land?

options.label: Its unusually cold temperature
The debris it picks up and carries
The salt it leaves on the soil
The loud roar that comes before it

items.explain: Tsunami water drags along debris as it moves over land, and that debris causes further damage.

items.prompt: A huge section of a glacier breaks off and crashes into the sea. Could this set off a tsunami that floods a coast?

options.label: No, only earthquakes cause tsunamis
No, ice floats so it moves no water
Only if it happens at high tide
Yes, by shoving aside a large mass of water

items.explain: Tsunamis form when a large body of water is displaced, and glacier calving is one way that can happen, along with earthquakes, landslides and eruptions.

items.prompt: After a severe coastal flood, which person is especially likely to suffer lasting mental health effects?

options.label: A healthy 30-year-old with family nearby
A tourist who left before the storm
An older adult who lives alone
A homeowner whose house stayed dry

items.explain: Anxiety, depression, grief and PTSD after floods can last months or years, and older adults and socially isolated people are particularly vulnerable.

items.prompt: During a storm, water keeps pouring over the top of a sea wall into town. Why can this end up threatening the wall itself?

options.label: The fast flow erodes the ground and undermines it
Salt in the water slowly dissolves the concrete
The water's weight pushes the wall out to sea
The town's drains back up and push on the wall

items.explain: Water flowing over a barrier moves fast enough to erode large amounts of land, which can undermine defense structures.

paragraphs.heading: A flood from the sea
paragraphs.text: A coastal flood is an event in which seawater covers dry, low-lying land by the shore. Storm surges from hurricanes and tropical cyclones, sea-level rise linked to climate change, and tsunamis can all set one off. The water can arrive by flowing straight in, by spilling over a barrier, or by breaking through it.

paragraphs.heading: Water over the wall
paragraphs.text: Overtopping happens when a barrier, natural or built, is topped by swollen seas in storms or at high tide, often along open coasts. The waves stand taller than the barrier, so water pours over it and floods the land behind. This flow can be very fast and can strip away a lot of ground, which can weaken the defences themselves.

paragraphs.heading: When a tsunami strikes
paragraphs.text: Tsunami waves cross the ocean after a large body of water is shoved aside by an earthquake, a landslide, a volcanic eruption or glacier calving. There is also evidence that meteors hitting the ocean caused big tsunamis in the past. They do so much harm because of their speed, their height when they reach land, and the debris the water drags along as it flows inland. The earthquake and tsunami in the Indian Ocean on 26 December 2004 were reported to have killed more than 200,000 people.

paragraphs.heading: Harm to the body
paragraphs.text: Apart from deaths, coastal floods cause injuries such as broken bones, cuts, burns, near-drowning and wounds from debris or collapsing buildings. They can make long-term heart, breathing and metabolic illnesses worse by cutting people off from their medicines and care. Hospitals often see more emergency visits afterward, and places with few resources carry a heavier load of flood-related illness.

paragraphs.heading: Disease and the mind
paragraphs.text: Flooding also raises the risk of infectious diseases, including cholera, dengue, hepatitis, malaria and typhoid. Dirty water, poor sanitation and more water where disease carriers can breed all play a part. Floods leave mental scars too, such as anxiety, depression, grief and PTSD, which can last for months or years. Children, older adults and people who are socially isolated are especially at risk.

paragraphs.heading: Costs to people and places
paragraphs.text: Lives, homes, businesses, roads, railways and industrial plants are all exposed, so the social and economic costs can be huge. Some losses are indirect: if valuable sandy beaches wash away, areas that depend on beach tourism lose visitors. The natural world suffers as well, since floods can destroy coastal wetlands and estuaries and wear away dunes.
